title: Container With Most Water: two-pointer from ends, move shorter side.
shortTitle: Container With Most Water: Two-Pointer From Ends
keyPoints: Area = min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left); limited by the shorter wall.
Start pointers at both ends and always move the pointer at the shorter line inward.
Moving the shorter side is the only move that can possibly increase the area, because moving the taller side only shrinks width without lifting the height cap.
O(n) time with O(1) extra space, beating the O(n squared) brute-force pair comparison.
When heights are equal, moving either side is safe because both are identically limited.
The correctness argument is that discarding the shorter line never loses a better answer because all pairs using that line as the limit have smaller width.

s1_definition.oneliner: Start pointers at both ends, area is shorter height times width, and always move the shorter side inward.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Container With Most Water** – given heights as vertical lines, find two lines forming the container holding the most water.
- **Area formula** – `min(h[left], h[right]) * (right - left)`; water is limited by the shorter wall.
- **Move-the-shorter-wall rule** – always advance the pointer at the shorter line; moving the taller line cannot increase area.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) space, versus O(n squared) brute force.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India plots Rajesh's monthly balances as a bar chart, and an analyst wants to know which two months, used as the left and right walls of a tank, would hold the most water between them as a visual measure of a sustained balance range. Two fingers start at the first and last month. The water held is limited by the shorter wall times the number of months apart. The analyst always moves the finger on the shorter wall inward, hoping to find a taller one.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  heights = [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]
             L                          R

  Step 1: L=0(1), R=8(7)  area = min(1,7)*8 = 8
          h[L]=1 < h[R]=7 --> move L

  Step 2: L=1(8), R=8(7)  area = min(8,7)*7 = 49
          h[L]=8 > h[R]=7 --> move R

  Step 3: L=1(8), R=7(3)  area = min(8,3)*6 = 18
          h[L]=8 > h[R]=3 --> move R

  Step 4: L=1(8), R=6(8)  area = min(8,8)*5 = 40
          h[L]=8 == h[R]=8 --> move R (or L)

  ... continue until L >= R
  Best area = 49  (lines at index 1 and 8)

  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Move rule:                      │
  │  shorter side --> MOVE INWARD   │
  │  taller side  --> KEEP          │
  │  equal        --> move either   │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Container With Most Water treats an array of heights as vertical walls and asks for the maximum water two walls can hold. I solve it with two pointers starting at the ends: compute the area (shorter height times width), record the best, and move the pointer at the shorter wall inward. It runs in O(n) time with O(1) space, beating the O(n squared) brute force.

The insight is why I move the shorter wall. The area is capped by the shorter wall, so moving the taller wall only shrinks the width while the height stays capped, and the area can never grow. Moving the shorter wall gives up width but is the only way to find a taller limiting wall that might compensate. That correctness argument, that discarding the shorter line never loses a better answer because all remaining pairs using it have smaller width, is what makes the linear scan valid.

When both heights are equal, moving either side is fine because any pair between them is limited by the same height with smaller width. For fewer than two lines I return zero since no container exists. For financial heights I use BigDecimal with compareTo and multiply for exact arithmetic.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this to power a balance-band visualisation, highlighting the two months forming the largest sustained balance band. The linear two-pointer approach made it responsive even over long account histories.

Remember one sentence: start two pointers at the ends, always move the shorter wall inward, and the area formula is min-height times width, giving the maximum container area in O(n).
